results.question: What do you build?
results.speech: My work is applied AI and agentic graph engineering. I build systems that map how a codebase fits together, and agents that make changes a team can check before it trusts them. I learned to build software before the AI era.

results.question: Why does graph engineering matter if AI can already read a repo?
results.speech: Graph engineering is the practice of making a codebase's structure queryable: parse it, store it as a graph, retrieve from it, and cite where each fact came from. Agentic graph engineering is building agents that use that graph before they change anything. My work is applied AI and agentic graph engineering.

results.question: What is GridSeak?
results.speech: Every structural claim in GridSeak names its evidence tier. An edge from a tree-sitter parse, an edge found by grep, and an edge confirmed by the language server carry different weight, and GridSeak keeps them separate. Flattening all of that into "GridSeak says" is a mistake by the user of the tool.

results.question: What is GridSchool and who is it for?
results.speech: Most GridSchool code is private because it handles student data. The GridSchool price is quoted on a call. You can book a call from gridschool.org. Earlier versions of GridSchool were a 12-month residency with a fixed curriculum and a shared multiplayer world.

results.question: How long is the GridSchool residency?
results.speech: Earlier versions of GridSchool were a 12-month residency with a fixed curriculum and a shared multiplayer world. The current residency is the 8-week route described here. The 12-month GridSchool residency and the shared multiplayer world are archived.

results.question: How do you check what an agent did?
results.speech: I also give agents narrow jobs with clear limits. A narrow agent with a fallback is far easier to trust than a general one. My view on agents and trust: a team should be able to check what an agent did before it trusts the change.

results.question: What's the difference between a junior using an agent and an excellent engineer using one?
results.speech: The difference between a junior using an agent and an excellent engineer using one is what happens after the output. The excellent engineer asks whether the change was verified, what it missed, and what a graph of the code would have shown before the money was spent.

results.question: Tell me about the job search engine you built for students.
results.speech: The Hire engine is the job-search system I built for GridSchool students. Its job is to take the busywork out of a job search so the student's time goes into the parts only they can do: preparing, talking to people, and doing the work. Each GridSchool student gets a daily run from the Hire engine, ordered by evidence.

results.question: What does your AI appointment setter do?
results.speech: The AI setter is an appointment-setting agent I built for GridSchool. When someone answers a GridSchool ad, the setter replies in chat, answers their questions about the residency, and books a call inside the conversation. The AI setter books calls directly into my calendar from the chat.

results.question: How does the map builder plan a route for each student?
results.speech: The map builder is the GridSchool system that drafts a custom route for each student. Given a student's goal, background, and current evidence, it picks and orders the modules into a route, and I review the draft before the student sees it. The student's home on GridSchool is the map.

results.question: What are you weakest at?
results.speech: Another weakness is that I have worked alone for a long stretch. That made me fast, and it also means I have had fewer people reviewing my code day to day than I would on a team. A third weakness: I have written long explanations when a short one would do.

results.question: What mistakes have you made building GridSchool?
results.speech: The biggest mistakes I have made as an engineer and founder fall into a few patterns, and I keep them written down so I can catch them early. I have over-abstracted. The correction was to talk to the people I wanted to serve, sell the simplest offer that helped them, and build only what that offer needed.

results.question: What kind of roles are you looking for?
results.speech: The roles I am looking for are applied AI engineer, agentic systems engineer, developer tooling engineer, and founding engineer at an early company. As an applied AI engineer, I want to work on the part of the product where a model meets real data and real users.

results.question: What's your tech stack?
results.speech: My main programming language is TypeScript. Most of what I ship today is TypeScript on the server and in the browser, including GridSchool, the Hire engine, and this portfolio. I also write Python, mostly for data work, scripts, and analysis around models.

results.question: How do you keep a RAG system from making things up?
results.speech: I start retrieval with lexical search like BM25 because it is cheap, deterministic, and easy to debug. The quality of a RAG system depends mostly on the source documents. Most RAG failures I have seen come from bad chunks and missing documents more than from the model.

results.question: How does this site keep the model cost bounded?
results.speech: AI Aden runs on Anthropic's Claude by default, and I can swap the model through configuration. The model fills a fixed schema and never writes code. Each visit gets five live questions to keep model cost bounded under a daily dollar ceiling.
